steps.name: Welcome
steps.text: New to Kotl? This tab takes you from account to first FireSim run. Use ◀ ▶ to step through.

steps.name: Account
steps.text: The admin adds you once (kotl-users, Slurm, the sudo rule). Then log in again so your shell has the group.

steps.name: Setup here
steps.text: On the workstation: kotl setup installs Kotl into your Claude Code and VS Code.

steps.name: Setup on your PC
steps.text: On your own PC: fetch the client bundle and run its installer; it reads Kotl over ssh.

steps.name: First job
steps.text: kotl run --eta 5m -- hostname: queued, a board claimed, a job key on its PC, your command runs, the board is freed.

steps.name: Watch
steps.text: The Kotl daemon refreshes a status file every second; the Claude band, the VS Code panel and kotl top show it.

steps.name: Results
steps.text: Each job leaves a private folder: kotl logs, kotl fetch, kotl history.

steps.name: FireSim
steps.text: Your own FireSim inside kotl run; the board is freed when runworkload returns.

steps.name: Rules
steps.text: Shared boards: always through Kotl, honest ETAs, release leases.

steps.name: Submit
steps.text: Claude runs kotl run --eta 1h -- firesim runworkload … over SSH. Kotl refuses a job without an exit plan (an ETA; --max defaults to 2× ETA).

steps.name: Queue
steps.text: The CLI hands the job to Slurm with sbatch. Slurm orders it by priority and estimates its start from the ETAs ahead of it.

steps.name: Start
steps.text: A board license frees up. Slurm's job starter runs job.sh, which hands over to Kotl's launcher.

steps.name: Claim board
steps.text: The launcher claims an idle, healthy board in the registry, marks it busy, and adds this job's key to the board's PC.

steps.name: Run
steps.text: Your command runs as you: your own FireSim, from your Chipyard. It reflashes the board and boots Linux, reaching the PC with the job key through the job's ssh-agent.

steps.name: Over ETA
steps.text: Still running past its ETA? Nothing is killed. The notifier (started every minute by a systemd timer) asks Slurm, then tells the owner and their Claude.

steps.name: Hang
steps.text: A guard trips: the owner's --max. The end step stops the simulation, removes the job key, marks the job over max, and tells the owner.

steps.name: Power off
steps.text: Normal end: the simulated Linux powers off, FireSim's runworkload returns, and the command exits. The launcher reads an optional KOTL RESULT line, removes the job key and frees the board. Slurm records succeeded or failed; its epilog repeats the end step as a backup.

steps.name: Results
steps.text: The collect step fills the job folder. Claude runs kotl fetch to pull it to the user's PC.

steps.name: Meanwhile
steps.text: Every 5 minutes Slurm runs Kotl's health check, which probes the board over the SSH path and marks a bad one down.

steps.name: Request
steps.text: You run kotl lease --eta 2h. It goes into the same Slurm queue as every job.

steps.name: Start
steps.text: Your turn: Slurm starts the lease. The launcher claims the board and adds this lease's key to its PC.

steps.name: Work
steps.text: ssh vcu118-pc1 uses your job key; ssh-add /tmp/kotl-keys-$USER/vcu118-pc1 gives it to FireSim or any tool. Run what you like.

steps.name: Over ETA
steps.text: Still working past your ETA? You get a notice, and the queue gets new estimates. Nothing is killed.

steps.name: Release
steps.text: kotl release: the end step removes the key, stops simulations left running and frees the board. Slurm's epilog repeats it as a backup.

steps.name: Forgot
steps.text: Walked away? When nothing of yours has run on the PC for the idle time (30m), the launcher ends the lease, frees the board and tells you. --max caps it either way.

steps.name: Request
steps.text: You run kotl board program vcu118-pc1 --bitstream new.bit. It becomes a Slurm job at the admin-only maintenance level.

steps.name: Drain
steps.text: Slurm starts it when it's first in line; the launcher marks PC 1 draining in the registry. A running job there finishes normally, or you cancel it.

steps.name: Program
steps.text: The launcher runs the Program / reset adapter, which loads the bitstream over the kotl SSH path.

steps.name: Verify
steps.text: The board-test adapter checks XDMA with a quick DMA read/write, and the health check confirms the board.

steps.name: Return
steps.text: The registry records the new bitstream and marks PC 1 idle. Users' jobs flow back in, and you get a done notice.

steps.name: Summary
steps.text: What Kotl installs or edits on each machine. Every change is made by a deploy/ script that the admin runs, and each script can undo its own changes.

steps.name: Workstation
steps.text: The workstation carries almost everything: Slurm, MariaDB, the kotl account, Kotl's programs and a few small config snippets.

steps.name: FPGA PC
steps.text: On the PC: a kotl account, one helper script and one sudoers line. sshd stays as it is until full lockdown.

steps.name: Users
steps.text: Nothing system-wide for users; their Chipyard is only read.

overview.title: Whole picture
bullets: Teal is Kotl, our product: the code we write and maintain, plus a plugin in each user's Claude.
Purple is Slurm, off the shelf. Kotl talks to it in exactly four places, through its normal commands.
Gray is everything else off the shelf (FireSim, the workstation's OS) and the hardware.
Everything reaching the FPGA PCs goes through the kotl key or a job key that works only while that job runs.

Users keep their own Chipyard and FireSim and run them unchanged inside a generic lease: kotl run -- <command> ends when the command exits, kotl lease ends on release. Kotl enforces an exit plan, not FireSim.
The core is a generic board lease (queue, claim, SSH access, end step). Adapters are admin board care, later: FireSim (flash, recover), program/reset, board tests.
overview.hint: New to Kotl? Open Guides and start with New user: start here. The sidebar lists every part by group; click a group to see what's inside, and a part for what it does, its commands and its files. Build status and history sit in each part's disclosures; Progress shows them all by milestone.

kotllens.title: What's Kotl
kotllens.what: Everything highlighted in teal: the code we write, install and maintain.
bullets: Entry: the kotl CLI (run, lease, release, status, fetch), console attach, and the Kotl plugin for Claude Code.

Core: the Kotl daemon (kotld, the one always-running process), the board lease (launcher + PC access), board registry, health check, ETA notifier, job results, the kotl SSH key. Later: power monitor, usage dashboard. Parked: same-design pick.

Adapters: task-specific knowledge, kept out of the core and switched on in kotl.conf. FireSim (built): XDMA and glibc checks, the XDMA repair, its cleanup and console. Later: program/reset, board tests. kotl run and kotl lease work for any tool without them.
kotllens.note: Not Kotl: Slurm (scheduling), each user's FireSim (simulation), the workstation OS (sudo, systemd timers, OpenSSH) and the FPGA PCs. Kotl only uses their normal commands and config files.

slurmlens.title: Where Kotl meets Slurm
slurmlens.what: Four places, numbered like the purple badges. Everything else in Kotl never talks to Slurm.
ordered: Queue ↔ kotl CLI. The CLI submits (sbatch), cancels (scancel) and lists (squeue). Slurm orders the queue by priority and counts boards as licenses.

Job starter → launcher. When a board is free, Slurm runs job.sh, which asks Kotl's launcher to claim it. A cancel arrives as a signal. After the job, Slurm's epilog runs Kotl's end step again as a backup.
Health runner → health check. Slurm runs Kotl's health.sh every 5 minutes.

Accounting → notifier and dashboard. The notifier asks who is running and when queued jobs will start; the dashboard (later) reads history with sacct. The Kotl daemon reads the queue every second (squeue) for the shared status file.
slurmlens.note: Kotl never changes Slurm's code. It only uses Slurm's commands and a few lines of slurm.conf.

remote.title: Remote user PC
remote.what: A user's own machine. Builds happen here; runs happen through the workstation.
bullets: Builds the design with their own Chipyard and FireSim (bitstream + driver).
Has a normal Linux account on the workstation, reached over SSH.
Never holds a lasting key to the FPGA PCs; a job key works only during their job.
What they get: kotl run and kotl lease for any tool, and Claude knows how to use them.

local.what: Same flow, but the user is already logged into the workstation.
bullets: Builds with their own Chipyard on the workstation.
Runs kotl run -- … or kotl lease from the workstation, with their own tools.
Gets no more FPGA access than a remote user.

admin.title: Admin (you)
admin.what: Root on the workstation. Runs maintenance and hears about stuck jobs and sick boards.
bullets: Can cancel any job.
Gets the 2× ETA alerts and board-down alerts.
Runs maintenance through Kotl, so it never collides with a user's job.
Grants the "urgent" priority level.

plugin.title: Kotl plugin for Claude Code
plugin.what: Kotl's plugin for Claude Code. Every user installs it once; Claude then knows how to use the board queue, and sees the queue and your notices when a session starts.
bullets: Skill: kotl run (preferred) and kotl lease with an ETA and an exit plan; FireSim through Kotl, with an honest KOTL RESULT and the glibc workaround; fetch, then read status.json first.
SessionStart hook: the queue, the boards and your unread notices (shown, not marked read).
PreToolUse hook (Bash): asks before firesim infrasetup/runworkload/kill runs outside kotl run/lease, and says how to run it through the queue. A suggestion with a question, not a block.

kotl-band (a second, optional plugin): a live Kotl band above the Claude Code prompt, from kotl status --json every 30 s. Line 1: each board, who holds it, the job's kind and time used of its ETA, how many wait. Line 2: your jobs: how many, each running one's time of its ETA, each waiting one's estimated start and place in line; unread notices. /kotl-band refreshes, /kotl-band hide hides. Read-only.

VS Code extension (kotl.kotl-status): the same in VS Code's status bar, in any window: each board, who holds it and their time of ETA, how many wait, your job count, unread notices; the hover lists the queue with estimated starts and your place in line; a click opens kotl top. Install: code --install-extension /opt/kotl/kotl-status.vsix.
Anywhere: on the workstation it runs kotl; on a user's own PC it runs ssh $KOTL_SSH kotl … (set KOTL_SSH in ~/.claude/settings.json under env).
plugin.note: Convenience only. The SSH lockdown and the end step are the real enforcement.

cli.title: kotl CLI
cli.what: The one command for everything, and generic: it holds a board for whatever you run. It talks to Slurm's queue for you.
bullets: kotl setup installs Kotl into your Claude Code and VS Code (--undo removes it); kotl client-bundle does the same for your own PC.
kotl run --eta T -- CMD: holds a board while CMD runs; ends the moment CMD exits. Good for FireSim runs.
kotl lease --eta T: holds a board for work by hand; ends on kotl release, the idle guard, or --max.
Exit plan, always: the ETA is required, --max defaults to 2× ETA, and a lease always has an idle guard. A job without one is refused.
Inside a job your command gets an ssh-agent holding only the job key, and KOTL_JOB, KOTL_BOARD, KOTL_PC. Your configs aren't touched.
Cancel works only for the job's owner or root.

lines.k: # a FireSim run: the board is freed the moment runworkload returns

lines.c: kotl run --eta 1h -- sh -c "firesim infrasetup -c my.yaml && firesim runworkload -c my.yaml"

kotl board list | drain | resume | add

attach.title: Console attach
attach.what: Opens your job's console (a screen session) on its PC, with your job key. Which session comes from the enabled adapter (FireSim: fsim0); with none, the PC's only screen session.
bullets: Runs as you: ssh with only your job key (no agent, no other keys), then screen -x on the adapter's session.
Works only for your own running job, from the workstation (the job key lives there).
Ctrl-a d detaches; the simulation keeps running. In kotl top the key is a.

launcher.title: Launcher · board lease
launcher.what: The core of Kotl: a generic board lease. It knows nothing about FireSim. Slurm starts it for every job; it claims a board, gives the owner SSH access for the job's lifetime, and always cleans up.
bullets: Confirms the Slurm job is real and belongs to the caller.
Install: sudo deploy/kotl/install.sh --board vcu118-pc1=vcu118@vcu118-pc1 copies the package to /opt/kotl/lib (root-owned) and installs /opt/kotl/launch, the only program users may run as kotl.
Start: claims an idle, healthy board in the registry, then adds this job's key to the board's PC.
During: the owner's command (FireSim, Vivado, scripts, anything) reaches the PC with the job key, through an ssh-agent that job.sh starts for it.
The lease ends when the work ends: the command of kotl run exits (e.g. FireSim's runworkload returns after the simulated Linux powers off), kotl release, or cancel. No timer closes it.
Guards (the exit plan): --max (default 2× ETA) for every job; for a lease also idle: nothing of the PC account running on the PC for N minutes (kotl.conf, 30m).

End step, every time: remove the job key and stop the job's simulations on the PC (in full lockdown: every process of the PC account), record why, free the board. Slurm's epilog repeats it as a backup. A KOTL RESULT: PASS/FAIL line in the output sets the result.
Records setup time on every job, for the parked same-design idea.

registry.title: Board registry
registry.what: One record per board: its state, what's loaded on it, its health and power.
bullets: States: down → idle → setting up → busy → draining → maintenance → idle.
The launcher claims a board here in one step, so two jobs never share a board.
The health check and power monitor write to it; kotl board list reads it.
A single SQLite file. No service to keep running.

health.title: Health check
health.what: A Kotl script that Slurm runs every 5 minutes. It checks each board over the kotl SSH path.
bullets: Every 5 minutes, one ssh call per PC. Generic: reachable, the board type's card on PCI (VCU118: Xilinx). Each enabled adapter adds its own lines; the FireSim adapter adds XDMA loaded and the glibc version.
Failing on an idle board: each adapter may try one repair (FireSim: one XDMA reload), then the board is checked again. A board a job holds is never touched: its tools may be mid-setup.

Still failing and idle: the board goes down; a Slurm reservation holds its license so queued jobs wait instead of failing; the admin gets a notice. A busy board is never taken from its job: it goes down when the job ends.
Recovery: when the checks pass again the board goes back to idle, the hold is released, and the admin is told.
Warnings (the board stays in the pool): the adapters' (FireSim: glibc differs), and something running as the PC account on an idle board (soft lockdown).
health.sh always exits 0, so a PC problem never drains the workstation's own Slurm node.

notifier.title: ETA notifier
notifier.what: A short Kotl pass that a systemd timer runs every minute, as kotl. It reads Slurm and writes notices into each user's inbox. It never stops anything.
bullets: Job passes its ETA: the owner hears once. Nothing is stopped.
Job passes 2× its ETA: the owner and the admin hear once.
A queued job's start estimate slips by 15 minutes or more: its owner hears.
Board down or back up: the admin hears (from the health check).
Where: kotl notices, kotl top, the unread count in kotl status, and Claude (M5).

* 11-23 20:05  job 42 now expects to start at 21:10 (later than before: the job ahead runs past its ETA)

results.title: Job results
results.what: One folder per job, written by the launcher at start and at the end step.
bullets: Owner only (0700, owned by kotl): you read it through the launcher, which checks the job is yours. kotl logs JOB [-f] shows the output; kotl fetch JOB unpacks the whole folder into ./kotl-results/JOB/.
Remote users run the same over SSH (ssh ws kotl fetch JOB); the Claude plugin does it for them.
Other users can't see it. Deleted automatically after 30 days (keep_days in kotl.conf).

lines.c: kotl logs 1235 -f              # follow a running job

power.title: Power monitor
power.what: Reads each board's power on a timer. Never queued, never blocks a job.
bullets: A systemd timer starts it every minute; it reads over the kotl SSH path. No agent on the PCs.
Source to decide later: the board's on-board power sensors, or a smart PDU per PC.
Stores readings in the registry. Alerts if a board draws power while idle, or goes over a limit.

dashboard.title: Usage dashboard
dashboard.what: A small web page on the workstation. Build it once the queue is running.
bullets: Board-hours per user per week, from Slurm's history.
Queue wait times, and how often jobs overrun their ETA.
Board state history and power per board, from the registry.

affinity.title: Same-design pick
affinity.what: On hold: prefer a board that already has the job's bitstream loaded, to save setup time.
bullets: FireSim says to re-run setup before every simulation, so setup can't simply be skipped.
The registry already knows what's loaded, so this would only be a board-pick rule.
Revisit once recorded setup times show it's worth it. No priority boost either way.

fsmod.title: FireSim adapter
fsmod.what: Everything Kotl knows about FireSim, kept out of the generic core. Users still run their own FireSim, unchanged, inside kotl run or kotl lease; this adapter only lets Kotl check, repair and clean up after it.
bullets: Switched on in /etc/kotl/kotl.conf: adapters = firesim (install.sh --adapters firesim). Off, Kotl still runs leases and jobs on any board, with only the generic checks.
Checks (added to the health check's one ssh call): XDMA driver loaded (a failure); glibc on the PC vs the workstation (a warning: drivers built here won't start on an older glibc).

Repair (idle boards only, once per down period): kotl-xdma-reload on the PC loads XDMA exactly as FireSim's infrasetup does (xdma.ko poll_mode=1). Never while a job holds the board: FireSim reloads the driver itself during infrasetup.
End step: names what to stop on the PC: screen sessions fsim* and processes FireSim-*. kotl-keys on the PC stops them without knowing they're FireSim's.
Lease idle guard: FireSim-* processes count as work.
Console: kotl attach opens screen session fsim0.
Later, admin only: flash a known-good bitstream, recover a board after a crashed job, a short known-good simulation as a deep check.

lines.k: # its PC part, on each FPGA PC (sudo there):

lines.c: sudo bash pc-setup.sh            # kotl-xdma-reload + one sudoers line

program.title: Program / reset
program.what: Admin adapter on the lease: load a bitstream or reset a board outside FireSim.
bullets: Takes a lease at the admin-only maintenance level, after the board is drained, so it never interrupts a user.
Programs or resets over the job key, then records the new bitstream in the registry.
The lease's end step cleans up the same way as for any job.

drvtest.title: Board tests
drvtest.what: Deep check of an FPGA PC and its board, as an adapter on the lease, before the board goes back in the pool.
bullets: Loads the XDMA driver, runs a quick DMA read/write test, records the driver version.
Runs after maintenance, a PC reboot or a failed health check, and optionally on a schedule.
The 5-minute health check stays a quick core probe; this is the thorough one, holding a lease so it never meets a user's job.

lines.o: xdma loaded · DMA read/write ok · driver 2024.1

key.title: kotl SSH key · job keys
key.what: The only paths from the workstation to the FPGA PCs: Kotl's own key, and short-lived job keys that Kotl adds and removes.
bullets: The kotl private key lives in /home/kotl/.ssh, readable only by the kotl account. Kotl uses it to grant and remove job keys, for health checks and for cleanup.
A job key lets the job's owner and their FireSim into the PC's FireSim account, only while the job runs (see PC access).
FPGA PCs: in full lockdown only kotl, virtex-host (job keys) and the admin, keys only. In soft lockdown (now) virtex-host's password and existing keys still work.
A new PC joins by adding the kotl key, the key helper and a registry entry.

lines.c: ssh vcu118-pc1 hostname        # as a normal user, no job running

queue.title: Queue + priority
queue.what: Slurm's queue holds waiting jobs and orders them. Kotl's CLI uses it through normal Slurm commands.
bullets: Each board type is a license, counted per board (vcu118:1 today, one board). A job needs one to start.

Priority (rough sketch, tune later): fair-share + waiting time + an "urgent" level only the admin grants. Maintenance has its own admin-only level. Fair-share uses Slurm accounting (slurmdbd + MariaDB on the workstation).
The ETA is required and becomes the job's time limit; Slurm uses it to estimate start times.
Never kills a job for passing its ETA. Only the owner or root can cancel.

starter.title: Job starter
starter.what: The part of Slurm that runs each job and signals it. Here it runs only on the workstation.
bullets: When a board license is free, runs job.sh as the user; it asks Kotl's launcher (as kotl) to claim the board and grant access.
On cancel: sends a stop signal, waits up to 2 minutes (KillWait), then force-stops.
After every job, runs Kotl's epilog: the end step again, as a backup.
Records the job as succeeded or failed from the exit code.

runner.title: Health runner
runner.what: Slurm runs Kotl's health check every 5 minutes. Two lines of slurm.conf.

acct.title: Accounting
acct.what: Slurm's accounting database. Answers who is running, for how long and when queued jobs start, and keeps the history.

os.title: Workstation OS
os.what: The workstation's own Linux pieces that Kotl relies on.
bullets: sudo: one rule lets users run exactly two Kotl programs as kotl.
systemd timers: start the notifier (and later the power monitor) every minute.
OpenSSH: carries the kotl key to the FPGA PCs.
Accounts: users in kotl-users; the kotl service account.
Full list of what Kotl changes here: the System files tab.

firesim.title: FireSim
firesim.what: Each user's own FireSim, in their own Chipyard, unchanged. Kotl doesn't install, wrap or change it: you run it inside a lease.
bullets: Run it with kotl run --eta T -- …firesim…: the board is held while it runs and freed the moment it exits.
Inside the job, FireSim reaches the PC through the ssh-agent job.sh starts (only the job key). Point your run farm at virtex-host@192.168.1.2, as your configs already do.
How the end is known: the simulated Linux powers off, FireSim's driver exits, runworkload sees the simulations finished and returns; Kotl sees the command exit.
A workload that never powers off keeps runworkload waiting; then --max ends the job.

pc1.title: VCU118 PC 1
pc1.what: Hosts the lab's VCU118, at 192.168.1.2 (vcu118-pc1 in kotl's SSH config). Reachable only from the workstation.
bullets: Runs sshd, the XDMA driver, FireSim's helper scripts and a small key helper. No other Kotl code.
Accounts: kotl, virtex-host (FireSim; gets job keys) and the admin.

Soft lockdown for now: password logins to virtex-host still work for people who know it. Take a lease (kotl lease) before touching the FPGA, or you may break a running job. Later: full lockdown with a separate admin account.
Reboots are harmless: the health check sees it come back.

pc2.title: VCU118 PC 2
pc2.what: Later: a second VCU118 PC. Same as PC 1 when it arrives; then the license goes to vcu118:2.

tooling.title: Repo tooling
tooling.what: What keeps this view honest: the status file, test tags and a commit check. Not drawn on the diagram.
bullets: status.json next to this page holds every part's build status.
Every test is tagged with the part it covers; tools/status.py turns test results into tested or failing.
A pre-commit check refuses a commit that changes a part's code without updating its status.

more.title: More boards
bullets: Add a PC: sshd + driver, the kotl key, a registry entry, and one more Slurm license.
Different board types get their own license name (for example u250:2).
Servers without FPGAs can join for health and power monitoring only.

access.title: PC access (job keys)
access.what: Lets a job's owner, and their own FireSim, reach the board's PC for exactly as long as the job runs. No timers: access follows the job.
bullets: Job start: job.sh makes a fresh ed25519 key as the user (the private half never leaves their account). The launcher checks it is one bare ed25519 key and adds it for virtex-host through kotl-keys, with restrict,pty.

Job end (the command exits, kotl release, cancel or a guard): kotl-keys remove takes the key out and stops what the enabled adapters name (FireSim: its fsim* screens and FireSim-* drivers); in full lockdown it also ends every virtex-host process. Soft lockdown can't tell a job's ssh shells from password shells, so those stay (they can't log in again).
Backup: Slurm's epilog runs the same end step after every job, even if the launcher crashed. It is safe to run twice.
Only the board this job claimed gets the key. Outside a job, users can't reach any PC.

Lockdown mode (lockdown in /etc/kotl/kotl.conf): soft (now): password logins to virtex-host still work and other keys stay; the end step kills only this job's sessions and simulations. full (later): separate admin account, virtex-host key-only, end step kills every virtex-host process.

daemon.title: Kotl daemon (kotld)
daemon.what: Kotl's one always-running process: a small systemd service, run as kotl, that runs tasks on their own intervals. More tasks join it later.

If it stops: systemd restarts it within 2 s; meanwhile every reader falls back to asking Kotl directly (slower, same answers). A task's error never stops the daemon; it shows in kotl daemon.

nu-welcome.title: New to Kotl? Start here

2 · Setup: one command puts Kotl into your Claude Code and VS Code (on the workstation, or on your own PC).
3 · First job: kotl run --eta 5m -- hostname.

5 · Results, then FireSim and the house rules.

jobsh.name: job.sh
jobsh.desc: What Slurm runs for every Kotl job, as the user: start (claim), your command, end step
jobsh.body:
#!/bin/bash
# managed by kotl (deploy/kotl/install.sh)
# What Slurm runs for every Kotl job, as the submitting user, inside their job:
#   1) the launcher (as kotl) checks the job is yours, claims a board, starts the guards
#   2) your command runs as you; its output goes to the job's output.log
#   3) the end step: frees the board and writes status.json (Slurm's epilog repeats it)
# Settings come from the kotl CLI: KOTL_MODE (run|lease), KOTL_MAX and KOTL_IDLE (seconds).
set -u
JOB=${SLURM_JOB_ID:?not inside a Slurm job}
read -r -a LAUNCH <<<"${KOTL_LAUNCH:-sudo -n -u kotl /opt/kotl/launch}"

"${LAUNCH[@]}" start "$JOB" --mode "${KOTL_MODE:-run}" \
  ${KOTL_MAX:+--max "$KOTL_MAX"} ${KOTL_IDLE:+--idle "$KOTL_IDLE"} --command "$*" || exit 1

stopping=0 pid=""
on_stop() { stopping=1; [ -n "$pid" ] && kill -TERM "$pid" 2>/dev/null; }
trap on_stop TERM INT HUP

# your command's output goes through a pipe to the launcher, which owns the log file
fifo=$(mktemp -u "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/kotl-$JOB.XXXXXX")
mkfifo -m 600 "$fifo"
"${LAUNCH[@]}" log "$JOB" <"$fifo" &
logpid=$!
"$@" >"$fifo" 2>&1 &
pid=$!
rc=0
while :; do
  wait "$pid"; rc=$?
  kill -0 "$pid" 2>/dev/null || break   # wait returns early when a signal arrives
done
# let the log writer drain (at most 10 s, in case something still holds the pipe open)
for _ in $(seq 1 50); do kill -0 "$logpid" 2>/dev/null || break; sleep 0.2; done
kill "$logpid" 2>/dev/null; wait "$logpid" 2>/dev/null
rm -f "$fifo"

if [ "$stopping" = 1 ]; then
  "${LAUNCH[@]}" end "$JOB" --signal
else
  "${LAUNCH[@]}" end "$JOB" --rc "$rc"
fi
exit "$rc"

skill.name: SKILL.md
skill.desc: Teaches Claude kotl run / lease with an ETA and an exit plan, FireSim through Kotl, and the fetch-then-read-status workflow
skill.body:
---
name: kotl
description: Use the lab's FPGA boards (VCU118) through Kotl, the lab's board queue. Use whenever a task runs anything on an FPGA board or its PC (FireSim infrasetup/runworkload, a bitstream, a driver test, ssh to an FPGA PC), or when the person asks about the board queue, their Kotl jobs, results, logs or notices.
---

# Kotl: the lab's FPGA board queue

The FPGA boards are shared. Kotl queues every use of a board through Slurm, gives the job SSH
access to the board's PC only while it runs, and frees the board the moment the job ends.
**Never use a board outside Kotl** (no plain `firesim infrasetup`/`runworkload`, no direct ssh to
an FPGA PC without a lease): it can break someone else's run.

## Where to run `kotl`

- On the workstation (`command -v kotl` finds it): run `kotl ...` directly.
- On a user's own PC: run it over ssh, `ssh "$KOTL_SSH" 'cd <folder> && kotl ...'`.
  `KOTL_SSH` is the workstation's ssh name (set in `~/.claude/settings.json` under `env`). If it
  is unset, ask the person for it. Files and folders must exist on the workstation.

## Every job needs an ETA and an exit plan

- `--eta` is required: your honest estimate. It only orders the queue; it never kills the job.
- `--max` (default 2x ETA) stops a hung job. Set it when a run might legitimately take longer.
- The job must end by itself: a command that exits, or a lease that is released.

## Run a command on a board: `kotl run` (preferred)

The board is held while the command runs and freed the moment it exits.

```sh
kotl run --eta 30m -- <command>
```

- Inside the job, the command has `KOTL_JOB`, `KOTL_BOARD`, `KOTL_PC` (user@address of the board's
  PC) and an ssh-agent holding only the job key: `ssh "$KOTL_PC" ...` works, FireSim's own ssh too.
- Exit code 0 = `succeeded`. A line `KOTL RESULT: PASS` or `KOTL RESULT: FAIL` in the output sets
  `passed`/`failed` instead. Print one when the exit code alone can't tell (see FireSim below).
- `kotl run` waits and streams the output. For a long run, add `--no-wait` (it prints the job
  number), then follow with `kotl logs JOB -f` or check `kotl status`. Run long waits in the
  background rather than blocking the conversation.

### FireSim

Run FireSim from the person's own Chipyard, with their environment active (`source env.sh` and
`sourceme-manager.sh --skip-ssh-setup` in the same shell), from `sims/firesim/deploy`:

```sh
kotl run --eta 30m -- sh -c "firesim infrasetup -c CFG && firesim runworkload -c CFG"
```

- The workload must power off by itself (FireMarshal `run`/`command`, or a script ending in
  `poweroff`); otherwise `runworkload` waits until `--max` stops the job.
- `runworkload` reports "completed" even when the driver failed to start: check the uartlog in
  `results-workload/<newest>/*/uartlog` and print `KOTL RESULT: PASS` only if it shows the real
  end (e.g. `reboot: Power down`). The lab's `deploy/examples/firesim-smoke.sh` does this.
- If `kotl board list` warns that glibc differs between the workstation and the PC, FireSim's
  bundled glibc must be removed on the PC after infrasetup: use
  `deploy/examples/firesim-smoke.sh --use-pc-glibc CFG`, or
  `ssh "$KOTL_PC" "cd <sim dir>/sim_slot_0 && rm -f libc.so.6 libm.so.6 libpthread.so.0 libdl.so.2 librt.so.1"`
  between the two commands.

## Work by hand: `kotl lease`

```sh
kotl lease --eta 1h        # waits for a board, then prints how to reach it
ssh <board>                # e.g. ssh vcu118-pc1: uses the lease's job key
kotl attach                # FireSim's console (Ctrl-a d detaches)
kotl release               # ALWAYS release when done
```

A lease ends on `kotl release`, after 30 minutes with nothing of yours running on the PC, or at
`--max`. If you start a lease for the person, release it when the work is done.

## Check, follow, fetch

| Need | Command |
| --- | --- |
| queue, boards, unread notices | `kotl status` (live view for a person: `kotl top`) |
| your past jobs and results | `kotl history` |
| output of a job | `kotl logs JOB` (`-f` follows a running one) |
| everything a job left | `kotl fetch JOB` -> `kotl-results/JOB/` with `status.json`, `output.log`, `launcher.log`, `outputs/` |
| cancel your job | `kotl cancel JOB` |
| notices (ETA passed, start slipped, board down/up) | `kotl notices` (marks them read) |

After a job ends: fetch it, read `status.json` first (`result`, `rc`, `reason`), then
`output.log`, then `launcher.log` (what Kotl did: key added/removed, guards, end). Report the
result, how long it took against the ETA, and anything odd.

## Results

`passed` / `failed` (KOTL RESULT line), `succeeded` / `failed` (exit code), `over_max` (the --max
guard stopped it), `idle` (a lease with nothing running), `released`, `cancelled`, `killed`
(ended by Slurm's backup), `no_access` (the board's PC couldn't be reached).

## Don'ts

- Don't run FireSim or touch an FPGA PC outside a Kotl job or lease.
- Don't cancel other people's jobs (Kotl won't let you anyway).
- Don't leave a lease running: release it.
- Don't guess an ETA of hours for a minutes-long run: ETAs order the queue for everyone.

kotlkeys.name: kotl-keys
kotlkeys.desc: The only Kotl code on a PC: adds and removes job keys for virtex-host; stops what the adapters name. Knows no tool
kotlkeys.body:
#!/bin/sh
# managed by kotl (deploy/pc/setup.sh). Installed on each FPGA PC as /usr/local/bin/kotl-keys.
# Runs as the PC's board account (virtex-host), started by the kotl account through sudo.
# Generic: what a tool leaves running (FireSim's screens and drivers) is named by the workstation's
# adapters, as --screen/--proc arguments; this script knows no tool.
#
#   kotl-keys add JOB 'ssh-ed25519 KEY'   let this job's key in (no forwarding; a terminal is allowed)
#   kotl-keys remove JOB [soft|full] [--screen PREFIX]... [--proc PATTERN]...
#                                         take the key out, quit the named screen sessions and stop
#                                         the named processes; full lockdown ends every process
#                                         of this account
#   kotl-keys list                        jobs whose keys are in
#   kotl-keys busy [--proc PREFIX]...     "busy: NAME, NAME" if remote work of this account runs here
#                                         (SSH sessions and what they started, screen, tmux, and the
#                                         named processes; not a local desktop login), else "idle":
#                                         the lease idle guard and the health check's warning
#
# Only lines ending in "kotl-job-<JOB>" are ever touched; every other key stays.
set -eu
umask 077
ME=$(id -un)
HOMEDIR=$(getent passwd "$ME" | cut -d: -f6)
# tests only: sudo resets the environment, so these can't be set in real use
HOMEDIR=${KOTL_KEYS_TEST_HOME:-$HOMEDIR}
AK="$HOMEDIR/.ssh/authorized_keys"
mkdir -p "$HOMEDIR/.ssh"
[ -e "$AK" ] || : >"$AK"

die() { echo "kotl-keys: $*" >&2; exit 2; }
job_ok() { case "${1:-}" in ''|*[!0-9]*) die "bad job id '${1:-}'" ;; esac; }
strip() {   # drop this job's lines, keep everything else and the file itself
  tmp=$(mktemp "$AK.XXXXXX")
  grep -v " kotl-job-$1\$" "$AK" >"$tmp" || true
  cat "$tmp" >"$AK"
  rm -f "$tmp"
}

# --screen/--proc NAME pairs after the fixed arguments; names are plain words only
SCREENS="" PROCS=""
names() {
  while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
    case "$1" in
      --screen|--proc)
        case "${2:-}" in ''|*[!A-Za-z0-9_.-]*) die "bad name '${2:-}' for $1" ;; esac
        if [ "$1" = --screen ]; then SCREENS="$SCREENS $2"; else PROCS="$PROCS $2"; fi
        shift 2 ;;
      *) die "unknown argument '$1'" ;;
    esac
  done
}

exec 9>"$HOMEDIR/.ssh/.kotl-keys.lock"
flock 9

case "${1:-}" in
  add)
    job_ok "${2:-}"
    printf '%s\n' "${3:-}" | grep -Eqx 'ssh-ed25519 [A-Za-z0-9+/]+={0,3}' || die "the key must be one ssh-ed25519 public key"
    strip "$2"
    printf 'restrict,pty %s kotl-job-%s\n' "$3" "$2" >>"$AK"
    chmod 600 "$AK"
    ;;
  remove)
    job_ok "${2:-}"
    JOB=$2 MODE=soft
    shift 2
    case "${1:-}" in soft|full) MODE=$1; shift ;; esac
    names "$@"
    strip "$JOB"
    [ -z "${KOTL_KEYS_TEST_HOME:-}" ] || { echo "would stop screens:${SCREENS:- none} procs:${PROCS:- none}"; exit 0; }
    # stop what the adapters named: their screen sessions, then their processes
    for p in $SCREENS; do
      screen -ls 2>/dev/null | awk -v p="$p" '$1 ~ "^[0-9]+\\." p { print $1 }' | while read -r s; do
        screen -S "$s" -X quit 2>/dev/null || true
      done
    done
    for p in $PROCS; do pkill -u "$ME" -f "$p" 2>/dev/null || true; done
    if [ "$MODE" = full ]; then
      exec pkill -KILL -u "$ME"   # full lockdown: nothing of this account outlives the job
    fi
    ;;
  busy)
    # Remote work only: processes in this account's SSH sessions, plus screen sessions, tmux
    # servers and the named processes (they outlive the ssh that started them). The PC's own desktop
    # login, if it runs as this account, isn't counted. This check itself isn't either.
    shift
    names "$@"
    mysid=$(ps -o sid= -p $$ | tr -d ' ')
    sshsids=$(ps -u "$ME" -o sid=,comm= | awk '$2 == "sshd" {print $1}' | sort -u | tr '\n' ' ')
    found=$(ps -u "$ME" -o sid=,comm=,args= | awk -v me="$mysid" -v ss=" $sshsids" -v procs="$PROCS" '
        BEGIN { n = split(procs, pp, " ") }
        $1 == me { next }
        index(ss, " " $1 " ") || $2 == "screen" || $2 == "SCREEN" || $2 ~ /^tmux/ { print $2; next }
        { for (i = 1; i <= n; i++) if (index($2, pp[i]) == 1 || index($0, " " pp[i]) || index($0, "/" pp[i])) { print $2; next } }' \
      | sort | uniq -c | awk '{print $2 ($1 > 1 ? " x" $1 : "")}' | paste -sd, - | sed 's/,/, /g')
    if [ -n "$found" ]; then echo "busy: $found"; else echo idle; fi
    ;;
  list)
    sed -n 's/.* kotl-job-\([0-9][0-9]*\)$/\1/p' "$AK"
    ;;
  *) die "usage: kotl-keys add JOB KEY | remove JOB [soft|full] [--screen P]... [--proc P]... | list | busy [--proc P]..." ;;
esac

xdmareload.name: kotl-xdma-reload
xdmareload.desc: FireSim adapter: the health check's one driver reload on an idle board, loading XDMA exactly as FireSim does (poll_mode=1)
xdmareload.body:
#!/bin/sh
# managed by kotl (deploy/adapters/firesim/pc-setup.sh). FireSim adapter. Installed on each FPGA PC as /usr/local/bin/kotl-xdma-reload.
# Kotl's health check runs it (as root, through one sudoers line, with no arguments) when the
# XDMA driver isn't loaded on an IDLE board: one attempt to reload it. It changes nothing else.
#
# It loads the driver exactly as FireSim's own infrasetup does (the same module, poll_mode=1):
# FireSim skips its own load when xdma is already loaded, so a driver loaded any other way
# (e.g. a plain `modprobe xdma`) would be the one FireSim runs on, and its simulation driver
# then can't find the card ("xdma_id != -1").
set -eu
KO="/lib/modules/$(uname -r)/extra/xdma.ko"
rmmod xdma 2>/dev/null || true
if [ -f "$KO" ]; then
  insmod "$KO" poll_mode=1
else
  modprobe xdma poll_mode=1
fi
lsmod | grep -q '^xdma '
echo "kotl-xdma-reload: xdma loaded (poll_mode=$(cat /sys/module/xdma/parameters/poll_mode 2>/dev/null || echo ?))"

clientinstall.desc: On a user's own PC: the Claude plugins, the VS Code extension, KOTL_SSH; --undo removes it all
clientinstall.body:
#!/bin/sh
# Kotl on your own PC: the Claude Code plugins (kotl, kotl-band) and the VS Code extension,
# reading Kotl over ssh from the workstation. Get this folder with:
#
#   ssh <workstation> kotl client-bundle > kotl-client.tar && tar xf kotl-client.tar
#   ./kotl-client/install.sh [--ssh <workstation ssh name>]     install (re-run after updates)
#   ./kotl-client/install.sh --undo                             remove it all again
#
# It keeps its files in ~/.kotl-client, sets KOTL_SSH for Claude Code (~/.claude/settings.json)
# and tells the VS Code extension the workstation's name (~/.kotl-client/ssh). Needs ssh to the
# workstation with a key (no password prompt), python3, and Claude Code and/or VS Code.
set -u
HERE=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)
DEST="$HOME/.kotl-client"
SSH=$(cat "$HERE/workstation" 2>/dev/null || true)
UNDO=0
while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
  case "$1" in
    --ssh) SSH=${2:-}; shift ;;
    --undo) UNDO=1 ;;
    -h|--help) sed -n '2,14p' "$0" | sed 's/^# \{0,1\}//'; exit 0 ;;
    *) echo "unknown option $1" >&2; exit 2 ;;
  esac
  shift
done

settings_env() {  # settings_env set NAME VALUE | settings_env unset NAME   (~/.claude/settings.json)
  python3 - "$@" <<'PY'
import json, os, sys
p = os.path.expanduser("~/.claude/settings.json")
os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(p), exist_ok=True)
try:
    s = json.load(open(p))
except (OSError, ValueError):
    s = {}
env = s.setdefault("env", {})
if sys.argv[1] == "set":
    env[sys.argv[2]] = sys.argv[3]
else:
    env.pop(sys.argv[2], None)
    if not env:
        s.pop("env")
json.dump(s, open(p, "w"), indent=2)
PY
}

if [ "$UNDO" = 1 ]; then
  if command -v claude >/dev/null; then
    claude plugin uninstall kotl@kotl >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "- Claude Code: kotl removed"
    claude plugin uninstall kotl-band@kotl >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "- Claude Code: kotl-band removed"
    claude plugin marketplace remove kotl >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "- Claude Code: marketplace removed"
    settings_env unset KOTL_SSH && echo "- Claude Code: KOTL_SSH removed"
  fi
  if command -v code >/dev/null; then
    code --uninstall-extension kotl.kotl-status >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "- VS Code: extension removed"
  fi
  rm -rf "$DEST" && echo "- removed $DEST"
  exit 0
fi

[ -n "$SSH" ] || { echo "give the workstation's ssh name: --ssh NAME" >&2; exit 2; }
echo "Workstation: $SSH"
if ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=5 "$SSH" kotl status --json >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "- ssh $SSH kotl: works"
else
  echo "! ssh $SSH kotl status failed: check you can ssh there with a key, and that you are in kotl-users"
fi

# a stable copy: Claude Code reads the plugins from this folder
if [ "$HERE" != "$DEST" ]; then mkdir -p "$(dirname "$DEST")"; rm -rf "$DEST"; cp -R "$HERE" "$DEST"; fi
printf '%s\n' "$SSH" >"$DEST/ssh"

if command -v claude >/dev/null; then
  claude plugin marketplace list 2>/dev/null | grep -q kotl || claude plugin marketplace add "$DEST" >/dev/null
  for p in kotl@kotl kotl-band@kotl; do
    claude plugin install "$p" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
    echo "- Claude Code: $p installed"
  done
  settings_env set KOTL_SSH "$SSH" && echo "- Claude Code: KOTL_SSH=$SSH"
else
  echo "- Claude Code: not installed here; skipped"
fi

if command -v code >/dev/null; then
  code --install-extension "$DEST/kotl-status.vsix" --force >/dev/null && echo "- VS Code: extension installed (reload the window)"
else
  echo "- VS Code: the 'code' command isn't on PATH; skipped (in VS Code: Shell Command: Install 'code' command, then re-run)"
fi
echo "Done. Start a new Claude Code session; in VS Code, Kotl is in the status bar and the Kotl panel."

fspcsetup.name: pc-setup.sh
fspcsetup.desc: Installs (or --undo removes) the adapter's PC part: kotl-xdma-reload and its sudoers line
fspcsetup.body:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# FireSim adapter, the PC part. Runs ON an FPGA PC, as root, with kotl-xdma-reload copied next to it.
#
#   sudo bash pc-setup.sh            installs /usr/local/bin/kotl-xdma-reload and one sudoers line:
#                                    kotl may run only that script, as root, with no arguments
#                                    (the health check's one XDMA reload on an idle board)
#   sudo bash pc-setup.sh --undo     removes both
#
# Needs Kotl's own PC setup first (deploy/pc/setup.sh: the kotl account). Add --dry-run to preview.
set -euo pipefail

HERE=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)
DRY=0 ACTION=install
say() { printf 'kotl-pc (firesim): %s\n' "$*"; }
die() { printf 'kotl-pc (firesim): error: %s\n' "$*" >&2; exit 1; }
run() { if [ "$DRY" = 1 ]; then printf 'would run: %s\n' "$*"; else "$@"; fi; }

while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
  case "$1" in
    --dry-run) DRY=1 ;;
    --undo) ACTION=undo ;;
    -h|--help) sed -n '2,9p' "$0" | sed 's/^# \{0,1\}//'; exit 0 ;;
    *) die "unknown option $1" ;;
  esac
  shift
done
[ "$DRY" = 1 ] || [ "$(id -u)" = 0 ] || die "run as root (sudo bash $0), or add --dry-run"

if [ "$ACTION" = undo ]; then
  run rm -f /usr/local/bin/kotl-xdma-reload /etc/sudoers.d/kotl-driver
  say "removed kotl-xdma-reload and its sudoers line"
  exit 0
fi

DRIVER="$HERE/kotl-xdma-reload"
[ -f "$DRIVER" ] || die "copy kotl-xdma-reload next to this script"
head -n 3 "$DRIVER" | grep -q 'managed by kotl' || die "$DRIVER is not Kotl's kotl-xdma-reload"
modinfo xdma >/dev/null 2>&1 || [ -f "/lib/modules/$(uname -r)/extra/xdma.ko" ] ||
  say "WARNING: no xdma module found here, so the reload can't work"
run install -m 755 -o root -g root "$DRIVER" /usr/local/bin/kotl-xdma-reload
rule='kotl ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/local/bin/kotl-xdma-reload ""'
if [ "$DRY" = 1 ]; then
  say "would write /etc/sudoers.d/kotl-driver (440): $rule"
else
  tmp=$(mktemp)
  printf '# managed by kotl (deploy/adapters/firesim/pc-setup.sh)\n%s\n' "$rule" >"$tmp"
  visudo -cf "$tmp" >/dev/null || { rm -f "$tmp"; die "sudoers line failed visudo"; }
  install -m 440 -o root -g root "$tmp" /etc/sudoers.d/kotl-driver
  rm -f "$tmp"
fi
say "kotl-xdma-reload installed; kotl may run it as root, with no arguments"
